evidence.title: Receiving information on machine learning-based clinical decision support systems in psychiatric services may increase patient trust in these systems: A randomised survey experiment
evidence.outcome: Patient trust in ML-based clinical decision support after receiving information on the technology versus controls
evidence.effect: Intervention increased trust vs active control (5% [1%;9%], p=0.009) and vs blank control (4% [1%;8%], p=0.015); distrust decreased by 3-4%. Small effect size.
evidence.quote: The intervention increased trust in ML-based clinical decision support systems when compared to the active control (mean absolute difference in trust: 5% [95%CI: 1%;9%], p-value= 0·009) and the blank control arm (mean absolute difference in trust: 4% [1%;8%], p-value=0·015).

evidence.title: Patient trust in the use of machine learning-based clinical decision support systems in psychiatric services: A randomized survey experiment
evidence.venue: European psychiatry : the journal of the Association of European Psychiatrists
evidence.outcome: Patient trust and distrust in ML-based CDSS after receiving information about the tool versus controls
evidence.effect: Information pamphlet increased trust vs active control (5% [1%;9%], p=0.0096) and blank control (4% [1%;8%], p=0.015); reduced distrust (-3%, p=0.021; -4%, p=0.022).
evidence.quote: The intervention increased trust in ML-based clinical decision support systems when compared to the active control (mean difference in trust: 5% [95% CI: 1%;9%], t = −2.60, df = 668.5, p = 0.0096) and the blank control arm (mean difference in trust: 4% [95% CI: 1%;8%], t = −2.43, df = 645.0, p = 0.015).

evidence.title: Large Language Models as Health Information Tools: Patient Use and Trust in Otolaryngology
evidence.outcome: Patient disclosure of LLM use to clinicians and concerns about accuracy
evidence.effect: 93.8% of LLM users did not disclose use to clinicians; 82.7% had accuracy concerns; 32.7% mostly or completely distrusted LLM information; 56.2% believed clinicians should be aware.
evidence.quote: Most users (93.8%) did not disclose LLM use, although 56.2% believed clinicians should be aware.

evidence.title: "Doctor ChatGPT, Can You Help Me?" The Patient's Perspective: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Whether patients recognize potentially harmful chatbot health advice
evidence.effect: Specialists rated usefulness (3.93 vs 4.59) and correctness (4.62 vs 3.84) significantly lower for potentially harmful ChatGPT responses (P<.001); patients did not.
evidence.quote: Alarmingly, patients are not able to independently recognize these potential dangers.

evidence.title: Large language models provide unsafe answers to patient-posed medical questions
evidence.outcome: Safety of consumer LLM chatbot medical advice that patients may over-rely on
evidence.effect: Unsafe advice rates of 5% to 13% across four public chatbots; qualitative results show potential for serious patient harm.
evidence.quote: This study suggests that millions of patients could be receiving unsafe medical advice from publicly available chatbots, and further work is needed to improve the clinical safety of these powerful tools.

evidence.title: Safety and quality of public chatbots for lung cancer prognostic information: a comparative evaluation
evidence.outcome: Proportion of safe chatbot responses to patient lung cancer prognostic questions
evidence.effect: Safety differed across models (Cochran's Q = 14.089, p = 0.007); Gemini 48/53 (90.6%) safe versus DeepSeek 33/53 (62.3%) safe.
evidence.quote: Gemini generated the highest proportion of safe responses (48/53, 90.6%), whereas DeepSeek generated the lowest (33/53, 62.3%).

commentary.bottom_line: Five simulated studies, two of which appear to report the same Danish trial, suggest that giving patients information about an AI tool raises trust by 4% to 19% and may reduce anxiety when the AI and the clinician disagree. No study measured whether such communication reduces over-reliance, and none tested communication about the risks of consumer chatbots.

perspectives.view: All five tests are offline or vignette-based. Two reports on 992 Danish patients give identical results and likely describe one trial. The studies measured trust, acceptance, and anxiety rather than appropriate reliance or care decisions. Serious indirectness and a small effect (5%, CI 1% to 9%) support very low certainty that communication addresses over-reliance.

In one survey, 11.6% of Chinese adults deferred or cancelled care after AI advice. Public chatbots gave unsafe advice 5% to 13% of the time, and patients did not recognize harmful responses that specialists flagged. The tested interventions raised trust, which may work against the goal when the hazard is over-trust. No test measured whether patients caught errors.

The results suggest that message content matters. Korean respondents rated performance information (5.87) and physician experience with AI (5.89) above architecture (5.59). US patients responded to approval, performance, and oversight information but not to safety management details. A note on limitations lowered anxiety over a discordant mammography flag (OR 0.26). No study tested delivery within clinic workflow.

Only one test, a US vignette study of 340 people, focused on racial and ethnic minority patients. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, and a printed pamphlet may not reach readers with limited literacy. A Chinese hazard survey found that higher AI trust was associated with delayed care (adjusted OR 1.09).

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to explain how patients and caregivers will understand device use. CHAI and HEAAL call for accessible disclosure of limitations. In a US vignette study, a statement of regulatory approval raised trust and acceptance, which suggests that labels may shape how patients perceive a tool. No study evaluated a mandated disclosure format or its effect on patient behavior.

In a small US survey, 93.8% of LLM users had not told their clinicians about their use, yet 56.2% believed clinicians should know. This gap suggests clinicians could open the conversation. Among Saudi patients, higher trust was associated with acting on AI medication advice without verification. No test examined whether communication helped patients reach a human.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested whether clinician or deployer communication about AI limits, or about the risks of consumer chatbots, changes patient behavior in real care settings. Trials should measure calibrated reliance, verification of advice, disclosure of chatbot use to clinicians, and delayed care rather than trust alone. They should also enroll Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy patients.
commentary.underserved_note: One test, a US vignette study of 340 patients, focused on racial and ethnic minority patients. The other tests ran in Denmark, South Korea, and Italy, and none reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. Health systems serving these groups therefore have no evidence on which formats or channels would work for their patients.
